big_idea: Building on The Innovator's Dilemma, Christensen and Raynor shift from diagnosing why incumbents fail to prescribing how established companies can successfully create and sustain new-growth businesses through disruptive innovation.

tool.label: Jobs to be done
tool.text: Rather than segmenting customers by demographics, the authors argue companies should identify the specific job a customer is trying to get done in a given circumstance, then design a product that does that job better than the alternatives, including non-consumption. The book's signature example is a fast-food chain's milkshakes: data showed many were bought alone, in the morning, by commuters, so the milkshake's real job was to be an easy, long-lasting, one-handed companion for a boring commute, not a dessert, redirecting improvement efforts toward thickness and drink-through time rather than flavor variety.
tool.note: Jobs to Be Done is closely associated with Christensen but was also developed and popularized in parallel by other practitioners, so attribution of the exact framework varies across sources.

ideas.title: Jobs to be done
ideas.text: Understanding the functional, emotional, and social job behind a purchase reveals opportunities that demographic segmentation misses entirely.

ideas.title: Low-end disruption
ideas.text: Targeting customers who are overserved by existing products with a simpler, cheaper offering that's good enough for their needs.

ideas.title: New-market disruption
ideas.text: Creating a product so much simpler or cheaper that people who previously couldn't participate in the market, non-consumers, now can.

ideas.title: Resources, processes, and values
ideas.text: An organization's capabilities and limits come from what it has, how it works, and what it prioritizes, and the same processes and values that enable core-business excellence often actively block disruptive initiatives.

ideas.title: Good money vs. bad money
ideas.text: Growth investments should be patient for growth, time to find the right strategy, but impatient for profit, a lean cost structure early, the reverse of how many companies fund new ventures.

ideas.title: Emergent vs. deliberate strategy
ideas.text: When a market is genuinely new, strategy should emerge from experimentation and learning rather than a fixed, upfront five-year plan.

try_it: Pick one product you sell and write down the actual job customers are hiring it for, in their own words and circumstances.
Look for a market segment your company treats as non-consumers and brainstorm a radically simpler offer that could reach them.
Audit whether a current growth project is funded like a sustaining project when it should be patient for growth, impatient for profit instead.
Identify one process or approval step from your core business that would slow or kill a genuinely new initiative, and ask if it needs its own separate path.
best_for: Senior leaders and innovation teams responsible for actually building new-growth businesses inside an established company
Product managers wanting a practical alternative to demographic segmentation
less_useful: Readers who haven't read The Innovator's Dilemma and want the underlying disruption theory explained from scratch, since this book assumes it
Very early-stage solo founders, since much of the advice concerns organizational structure and capital allocation inside larger companies

related.why: The original diagnosis of the disruption problem this book prescribes solutions for
A complementary organizational-design approach to running the new venture alongside the core business
